The White-bellied woodstar (Chaetocercus mulsant) is one of the smallest hummingbird species in the Andean cloud forests, and its life history reflects the extreme energetic demands of a miniature endotherm. Females construct a tiny cup nest in which they deposit two white eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two white eggs per clutch]. Field studies indicate that a single clutch is initiated each year [F_R_i = single clutch is initiated each year], a remarkably low reproductive frequency for a trochilid of this size. Respirometry trials conducted under controlled thermal conditions at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] have measured a maximum basal metabolic rate of 12.73 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 12.73 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that underscores the prodigious metabolic cost of hover-flight and nocturnal torpor in such a diminutive bird. This elevated oxygen consumption is comparable to rates recorded in other Andean emerald hummingbirds of similar body mass and is consistent with the high wing-beat frequencies required for sustained hovering in the cool, thin air of its montane habitat.

Hatchling mass is remarkably low, with neonates emerging from the calcareous egg at an initial weight of just 0.64 grams [Ww0 = 0.64 grams], a figure derived from allometric relationships observed in other tropical hummingbirds. The incubation period is relatively short; eggs maintained at a constant ambient temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C] complete development in 15 days [ab = 15 days], after which the altricial nestlings are entirely dependent on maternal provisioning. This brief embryonic phase likely reflects selection for rapid development to minimize predation risk during the vulnerable egg stage. The downy chicks exhibit a beak gape feeding response within hours of hatching, and their growth trajectory is steep, fueled by the female's frequent regurgitation of nectar and small arthropods. The trade-off between clutch size and offspring quality is evident here, as the energetic burden of provisioning two rapidly growing chicks must be balanced against the mother's own substantial daily maintenance costs.

Post-hatching development proceeds rapidly under the thermal conditions typical of the breeding season at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], a temperature that approximates the internal body temperature of an active adult. Fledging, defined as the achievement of first flight and nest departure, occurs at 17 days after hatching [tx = 17 days after hatching], a relatively brief nestling period that is characteristic of small trochilids at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This early departure minimizes cumulative exposure to nest predators but forces the young to navigate a challenging environment before they have fully mastered sustained flight. The pin-feathered chicks gain mass quickly, and parental provisioning continues for several days post-fledging as the juveniles refine their foraging skills. The rapid attainment of flight capacity is a critical adaptation for a species that occupies edge habitats and forest gaps where aerial agility is essential for both feeding and escape from predators.

Sexual maturity is not reached until considerably later than fledging; under the same thermal regime of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], puberty is attained at 51 days after hatching [tp = 51 days after hatching]. This developmental lag reflects the time required for complete ossification of the skeleton and full maturation of the flight musculature, both of which are essential for the demanding hovering and rapid acceleration maneuvers that characterize adult foraging. The onset of gonadal activity, marked by testicular enlargement in males and ovarian follicle development in females, signals the transition to a reproductively viable state. Interestingly, the attainment of sexual maturity does not immediately translate to breeding; first-year birds may delay reproduction while they establish territories and refine their floral resource utilization. The relatively early puberty compared to larger hummingbird species likely reflects the high adult mortality rate that selects for earlier reproductive investment.

Adult females achieve a maximum wet body mass of 4.5 grams [Wwi = 4.5 grams], while males are slightly smaller at 3.8 grams [Wwi = 3.8 grams], a modest sexual size dimorphism that is common among hummingbirds and likely related to differences in competitive regimes and display behavior. The cumulative mortality risk across these extended pre-reproductive and reproductive years is high, and the species’ persistence depends on a delicate balance between modest annual fecundity and the few surviving offspring that manage to recruit into the breeding population.
